author: Akien (the ruling and the worked inference) + CC (the capture)
text: SYSTEM METRICS SHOULD ALSO BE LEARNING. Akien, verbatim: 'system metrics should also be learning. we wanna watch what it costs to spin up another x, and in future be able to yeah/nay based on data, not a number out of akien's head. but even so, inference can be made: if no x running and 20% cpu, and 1 x = 30%, then we can say, from data, that we prolly don't wanna go over 6 x. keeping an eye on it as we go of course.' THE METHOD, abstracted: measure the BASELINE (the box with none of this thing running), measure the MARGINAL COST of one more, subtract a RESERVE (the headroom the host keeps for itself), and divide what is left by the margin — the ceiling falls out. Every term is observable; none is a number a person has to hold. Akien's own worked numbers: baseline 20%, +10 points per x (1x=30, 2x=40, 3x=50, 6x=80), 'and leave some headroom for the system' — (80 − 20) / 10 = 6. WHAT IT RETIRES: harbor_master's HARBOR_LINES, both values — cpu 75.0 (derived from Akien's measured 6-of-8 crawl point) and memory 1024 (a labelled hypothesis). It also puts a number on an assumption hiding inside the 75, that one builder costs one runnable: 10 points on 8 cores is ~0.8 runnable per builder, so his example is CONSISTENT with the assumption rather than against it. Consistent is not measured; nobody has measured it. THE SHAPE OF THE WHOLE THING: the 6/8 number was a LEARNED VALUE ALL ALONG — learned from experience, held in Akien's head, and written down nowhere in either repo before 2026-08-04. This is not new learning being invented; it is an existing learned value moving out of a human's head into data the system holds. And 'keeping an eye on it as we go' is the standing half: a marginal cost is not a constant either (it moves with whatever else lives on the host), so the ceiling is a live derivation, not a one-time calibration. CORRECTED SAME DAY, AND THE CORRECTION IS PART OF THE NOTE: I first read the '1 x = 30%' as the MARGINAL cost rather than the running total, which made the ceiling arithmetic come out at 200% and led me to write — here, in system_rackmount's charter, and into the session slate — that the inference was expressible only because runnable-over-cores has no 100% ceiling, and that the example implied ~2.4 runnable per builder. Both claims were mine and both are wrong; 80% sits under a 100% ceiling without trouble. Akien: 'the concept made it across even tho the math in my head didn't. And this failure of communication is exactly why it's a progressively closer process.' The loss happened at head→english, my capture was faithful to the wrong english, and the thing that caught it was restating the arithmetic back to him in my own words — which is the same correction loop as showing him a translation, just pointed at a number.
